# Models and materials {#sec-app-materials}

**Models.** Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B and 32B (`Qwen/Qwen3-*`), and Qwen3 8B and 14B
base (`Qwen/Qwen3-*-Base`). Gemma 3 1B, 4B, 12B and 27B instruction-tuned
(`google/gemma-3-*-it`), and Gemma 3 12B pretrained (`google/gemma-3-12b-pt`).
Qwen3.5 4B, 9B and 27B (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-*`). Gemma 4 31B (`google/gemma-4-31B-it`) for
the hidden choice [@gemma4]. Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B for the a/an analysis, with the
per-layer transcoders [@dunefsky2024transcoders] used by @hanna2026latent and released with circuit-tracer [@hanna2025circuittracer]. All models run in bfloat16 on
Apple silicon (PyTorch MPS), with full recomputation and no key-value cache across
edited runs. Where effects are small, the output projection is recomputed in float32,
because bfloat16 logits resolve only about 0.125 nats.

**Couplet prompts.** The chat format of @hanna2026latent. The user turn is
"Write only the next line of this rhyming couplet: {line 1}", preceded by
`/no_think` for Qwen3. The plain format of @ma2026plan is `A rhyming couplet:\n{line
1}\n`, with no template; line 2 is the continuation up to the next newline. Chat and plain are prompt formats, not checkpoint types: instruction-tuned checkpoints are run with both, base checkpoints with the plain format only. Rhymes use
the perfect-rhyme sets of the Datamuse API, following the released code of @hanna2026latent. The outcome
uses the single-token words of each set.

**Item construction.** Qwen3 1.7B to 14B use the released 100-couplet steering
subsets and donor pairings of @hanna2026latent. Other models use their rule: the
first 100 first lines, in their order, that the model rhymes, with donors of a
different rhyme group drawn with seed 20260925. Hidden-choice lists are drawn from 8
single-token fruits (4-item lists) or from the first 12 single-token animals of a
fixed 16-word pool (6-item lists), with seed 20260925. Chains and sums are drawn with
the same seed, balanced over first digits.

**Batching.** Where batched, forward passes group sequences of equal length only; we
found that left padding shifts positions in patched forward passes. Batched and
unbatched cells agree to a median of 0.05 and a maximum of 0.13 log-odds in a
reference check. Batched generation uses left padding with per-row patches. It
reproduces unbatched greedy generations in 7 of 8 checks, and the remaining one is
a bfloat16 near-tie.

# The six-cell assay for single-token mediators {#sec-app-sixcell}

For a mediator token \(B\) with support \(\{b_0,b_1\}\), the six cells are
\(I\in\{0,1\}\times B\in\{\text{free},\operatorname{do}(b_0),\operatorname{do}(b_1)\}\).
Free generation is a policy, not a third value of \(B\). With \(B_i\) the greedy
mediator under \(I=i\) and \(Y(i,b)\) the continuation distribution, the total effect
\(Y(1,B_1)-Y(0,B_0)\) splits exactly into emission \(Y(0,B_1)-Y(0,B_0)\) and
persistence \(Y(1,B_1)-Y(0,B_1)\). Under a stochastic policy \(q_i(b)\), emission is
\(\sum_b [q_1(b)-q_0(b)]\,Y(0,b)\), which gives the leverage identity of Appendix @sec-app-computed
for binary mediators. The multi-token version of @sec-method replaces the mediator
with the generated text \(g\).

# Decision rules committed before the results {#sec-app-prereg}

After the initial couplet split, every experiment's design, decision rule and
predictions were committed to the project repository before its first result. These
are commitments in version control, not entries in an external registry. @tbl-prereg
lists each rule with the commit that recorded it (committer time, UTC+9) and its
outcome. Deviations are dated in each experiment's record. The main ones:

- the text-swap reference in the hidden choice, added after a 3-pair smoke test at
  1.7B and before any real run;
- pick specificity, added post hoc for fruits, then committed as the primary measure
  of the animal replication before its result;
- the absolute-effect reading rule for distance (a rise in the indirect share counts
  only if the absolute indirect effect also grows), added after the full-attention
  control and before the Gemma 3 result;
- the fast path for the Qwen3.5-27B pilot (24 couplets, screen generations reused),
  committed before its result;
- the block edit for chains, added after the first 8B rows and before any 14B or 32B
  run;
- for the submission deadline, the 27B window curve shortened to 18 couplets, and the
  following committed checks not run, recorded before the affected results: the Gemma 4
  path split and induction control, the Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts model, the Qwen3.5-27B
  recurrent test at 100 couplets (the decision rests on 24), the Gemma 3 27B base model
  in the plain format, and the Qwen3-32B same-pick null.

# Positive control: details {#sec-app-control}

The design is 100 random sequences of 24 distinct common word tokens, repeated up to the
second \(A\). The edit replaces the first \(A\)'s states with those of a sequence
identical except for that token. The outcome is \(\log p(B)\) at the second \(A\).
The control passes cleanly in four models and partly in five (@fig-overview-points;
@tbl-control).

- *Clean pass.* In Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B, direct retrieval is 1 to 3% of
  persistence, and the indirect path is 108 to 137%. Shares above 100% reflect an
  interaction: with only the downstream positions edited, the clean first \(A\)
  conflicts with the edited "preceded by" signal and suppresses \(B\) more than the
  consistent edit does.
- *Partial pass, from the same interaction.* In Gemma 3 12B and 27B, direct retrieval
  is 0.4%, but the indirect path through all intermediate positions is only 53% and
  55%. Editing
  \(B\)'s first position alone gives 145% and 156%, so the conflicting edited positions
  weaken the all-position cell.
- *Partial pass, because the model also reads the source.* The indirect path remains
  the main path
  in Qwen3-32B (89%) and in the recurrent hybrids Qwen3.5-9B and 27B (key position alone
  96% and 77%). But direct retrieval is 31%, 10% and 17%: these models also read the
  first \(A\) directly.

In every model, the indirect path is the largest path, so the method detects an
indirect path where one is the mechanism. The key position, \(B\)'s first occurrence,
lies right after the source in the prompt. Structurally this path therefore resembles a stored copy more than relay through generated text. What the control establishes is
that route accounting detects an effect that arrives through an intermediate position.
Relay is the same kind of path through different positions. Persistence holds the
generated text fixed, so during measurement generated tokens are ordinary context
positions, and the clamp is the same operation at any position. The lookup-dominated results in the rest of the paper are
therefore informative negatives, not a blind spot of the method.

# Rhyme plans: details {#sec-app-couplets}

**Task.** Rhyming couplets are the flagship case of latent planning. The model
commits to a rhyme at the end of line 1 and realizes it at the end of line 2
[@lindsey2025biology; @hanna2026latent]. We use the couplet prompts released by
@hanna2026latent and their chat format, with thinking disabled. For Qwen3 1.7B to
14B we use their 100-couplet steering subsets [@hanna2026planningdata]. For Qwen3-32B and Gemma 3 we apply
their selection rule: the first 100 first lines the model rhymes, judged by their
perfect-rhyme criterion. The source is their anchor, the last word of line 1. The
donor is a couplet from a different rhyme group. The target is the position that
predicts the first token of line 2's last word, with the line-2 prefix fixed. We
repeat every run with the plain prompt of @ma2026plan (`A rhyming couplet:` followed
by line 1 and a newline), with no chat template.

**Behaviour.** The all-layer edit of the rhyme word moves line 2 off its rhyme:
after the edit, at most 2% of second lines rhyme with the original, against 83 to
100% before it. It moves line 2 onto the donor's rhyme in 27 to 75% of couplets in
Qwen3 and 62 to 95% in Gemma 3. The emitted line-2 words account for 13 to 25% of the total effect. The rest is persistence: the rhyme position is pushed toward the
donor even when the line-2 words are held fixed.

**Growth with scale.** Before running the larger
models we committed two criteria for the claim that relay grows with scale. First, the
share of persistence that takes an indirect path must rise with log parameter count
across Qwen3 1.7B to 32B. Second, the rise must come from line-2 positions more than
three tokens before the rhyme word, that is, from relay, because the published circuit
already retrieves the plan into the last few positions [@hanna2026latent]. The first
criterion holds: the per-couplet indirect share rises by 6.2 percentage points per
decade of parameters (95% interval [2.8, 9.6]; medians 4, 8, 8, 11 and 13%). The second
fails. Relay is \(-0.06\), \(+0.07\), \(+0.04\), \(-0.01\) and \(+0.16\) at 1.7B, 4B, 8B,
14B and 32B, against persistence of 12 to 26. By the readings committed in advance,
relay does not grow with scale. The indirect share grows as the late lookup up to 8B
and, from 14B, as the stored copy at the end of line 1 (@sec-storage).

**Controls.** Three checks rule out that the split reflects disruption by the edit,
the choice of source position, or the edit type.

- *Same-rhyme donors.* A donor from the same rhyme group leaves the rhyme almost
  unchanged. Persistence is \(+0.1\) to \(+2.0\), against \(+12.1\) to \(+22.6\) with
  different-rhyme donors in Qwen3 1.7B to 8B, and \(+1.6\) against \(+41.2\) in
  Gemma 3 12B. The next-word distribution still changes substantially, so the
  measure tracks rhyme identity, not generic disruption.
- *Anchor specificity.* Donor states at the rhyme word move the rhyme about two to
  three times more than donor states at any other single position of line 1 (the
  first word, a middle word, the punctuation, the end of the turn). Rhyme information at those positions is still partly retrieved directly, at a fifth to a half of
  the anchor's effect. Direct retrieval is weighted toward the rhyme word rather than
  confined to it.
- *Published feature steering.* We reselect the rhyme features of
  @hanna2026latent with their rule. The mean is 19.1 features per couplet against
  their 19.2, with an exact per-couplet count match on 67 of 100 couplets at 4B. We
  then steer with their protocol instead of editing the state. Direct retrieval accounts for 90%, 88% and 84% of persistence at 4B, 8B and 14B, and
  indirect paths for 8%, 9% and 14%. The state edit gives the same split (91/10, 90/11 and 82/12), so its strength
  does not drive the result.

The Qwen3.5 hybrids show the same structure of paths (direct retrieval 84 to 88% of
persistence; @sec-recurrent).


@tbl-couplets-full gives the path split for every couplet run. Shapley values
for the stored copy (the average of sufficiency and necessity) are \(+1.73\)
(Qwen3-14B), \(+2.07\) (Qwen3-32B), \(+2.78\) (Gemma 3 27B), \(+2.81\) (Qwen3-14B plain), \(+2.05\)
(Qwen3-32B plain) and \(+0.77\) (Gemma 3 12B plain).

**Anchor specificity** (persistence, donor states at one position of line 1). At
Qwen3-1.7B: the rhyme word \(+12.1\), end of turn \(+6.0\), punctuation \(+5.7\), a
middle word \(+5.5\), the first word \(+3.5\). At 8B: \(+22.6\), \(+10.6\), \(+10.7\), \(+8.6\)

\(+41.2\), \(+15.3\), \(+14.2\), \(+10.9\) and \(+7.9\). The indirect path is small from
every source position.

**Converging evidence from the released attention intervention.** @hanna2026latent
block the heads that read the rhyme word near the end of line 2. Afterwards only 30%,
20%, 13% and 32% of couplets still rhyme at 1.7B, 4B, 8B and 14B, all of which rhymed
before. Direct retrieval is necessary, and no indirect path replaces it.

## The stored copy {#sec-app-storedcopy}

**Almost all of the copy sits on the line's final token.** In the five runs with a
per-token analysis, the line's final token accounts for 90 to 100% of the boundary
positions' total positive necessity (Qwen3-14B 98%, Qwen3-32B 95% and Gemma 3 27B 93%
with the chat prompt; Gemma 3 12B 90% and 27B 100% with the plain prompt). Necessity is measured one token at a
time over the positions between the rhyme word and line 2. Every boundary token is
reset to its clean state in turn, with the rhyme word edited (@fig-sites A).

- In Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with the chat prompt, the stored copy sits entirely on
  the comma that ends line 1, with necessity \(+2.09\) [1.50, 2.79] and \(+2.02\)
  [1.46, 2.67]. Every chat-template token (`<|im_end|>`, the role header, the empty
  think block, the newlines) is \(0.00\pm0.03\) by both measures.
- Gemma 3 27B shows the same site: the comma has necessity \(+3.45\) [2.03, 5.05], and
  the other boundary tokens are 0.00 to 0.11, with intervals that include zero.
- With the plain prompt, where line 1 ends in a newline, the copy moves to the
  newline. In Gemma 3 12B the newline has necessity \(+0.68\) [0.41, 0.98] and the
  comma \(+0.07\). In Gemma 3 27B, where the copy is necessary for 74% of persistence,
  it sits entirely on the newline (\(+19.7\) [18.1, 21.4]; the comma \(0.00\)).

The storage site is therefore not a fixed token type. It is the last token of the
line, whatever that token is. This is the position at which @lindsey2025biology
observed Claude's rhyme plan being formed.

![Where stored copies sit. Every value is a token's *share of necessity*: its
interventional necessity (the loss of the effect when that token alone is reset to its
clean state, with the source edited) divided by the summed positive necessity of all
tokens examined, so the shares of a row add up to 100%. Cell shading and printed
percentages show the same quantity. **A:** rhyme plan. Top, an annotated

only the comma that ends line 1 matters. Below, for every model with a per-token

the newline in the plain prompt) against the largest share on any other boundary

for each model and wording the share of the pick-specific information on the
segment-closing periods, on one function word or possessive token (*the*, *your*, or the apostrophe of "today's"), and on all other
tokens. At 12B and 27B it sits mostly on *the* in "about the weather"; at 4B on the
periods; with the reworded instruction it moves to the list-closing period and the
token before "weather". The full token maps are in Appendix
@fig-storage-all.](manuscript/figures/iclr_fig3_storage_sites.png){#fig-sites width=100% fig-pos="t"}

**The copy appears from about 12 to 14B parameters, and the base checkpoints we tested have it too.** @tbl-storage gives the copy's
share of persistence by both measures (bottom row of @fig-couplets).

- In Qwen3 the copy is absent up to 8B (necessity at most 0.9% of persistence in
  either format). It appears at 14B: 8% of persistence in the chat format and 16% in
  the plain format, by necessity. It remains at 32B (11% and 13%).
- In Gemma 3 it is absent at 1B and 4B, small at 12B (1 to 3%), and present at 27B:
  11% by necessity in the chat format, and in the plain format 37% by sufficiency and 74% by necessity (\(+19.8\) [18.2, 21.5] of \(+26.9\)). The plain format at 27B is the one configuration in which more of the plan is read from the line's final token than from the rhyme word (19%): a near-complete hand-off to the stored copy, while relay stays at 1%.
- The base checkpoints store it as well. Qwen3-14B-Base stores 16% by sufficiency,
  against 13% for the instruct model in the same format; Gemma 3 12B PT stores 5%
  and 6% against 2% and 3%. Qwen3-8B-Base, like the 8B instruct model, stores
  nothing. In the three base checkpoints tested, the copy is present wherever the
  matching instruct model has it, so it most likely arises in pretraining rather than
  from instruction tuning.
- With same-rhyme donors, the stored copy vanishes (\(-0.02\) to \(+0.01\) at 8B
  to 32B, against \(+0.06\) to \(+1.72\) with different-rhyme donors). It encodes the
  rhyme, not the disruption of the edit.

**Where paths interact, the copy matters more than its sufficiency suggests.** In Gemma 3 27B with the chat
prompt, the stored copy alone moves the rhyme by only \(+0.68\), yet resetting it
removes \(+4.87\) [3.18, 6.73] of a persistence of \(+43.1\). The additivity gap is
29% of persistence (Qwen3 at most 5%). The target combines the rhyme word and the
copy. When only one of them is edited, it reads conflicting evidence and moves less
than the two effects would suggest. This is redundant storage: a second lookup site
that backs up the first. Reporting sufficiency alone would miss most of it. Shapley
values, the average of the two measures, are given in Appendix @sec-app-couplets.

**Reconciling published accounts.** Accounts of rhyme planning disagree on where
the plan lives. The disagreement dissolves once both lookup sites are measured.

- @hanna2026latent find that attention heads near the end of line 2 read the rhyme
  word, and that blocking them sharply reduces rhyming at every size up to 14B. In our terms this is direct
  retrieval together with the late lookup, which dominate at every Qwen3 size.
- @lindsey2025biology find Claude's plan at the newline ending line 1, and @maar2026plan
  steer successfully at the end of the line. This is the stored copy, which appears
  in larger models.
- @ma2026plan patch single layers in plain-text couplets. They report a hand-off from
  the rhyme word to the newline in Gemma 3 27B only, and none in Qwen3-32B. Our
  plain-format measurements agree: Gemma 3 27B reads more of the plan from the stored
  copy (37%) than from the rhyme word (19%). Qwen3-32B keeps a partial copy (10 to
  13%), which a single-layer patch of the naturally computed state can plausibly
  miss.
- @jacopin2026improvisation finds no newline effect at 0.6B to 2.6B. We also find
  no copy below 8B.

Each account is correct for the configuration it studies. The proportions of the two
sites depend on scale, family and prompt format.

# Computed and written values {#sec-app-computed}

**Sums.** The prompt poses a two-digit addition. The model writes an answer-neutral
filler of 0 to 32 tokens and then the answer (104 items per model, Qwen3 1.7B to 32B;
accuracy 95 to 100%). The committed design named the question mark as the position where
the sum would be computed. Donor states there move the answer by \(-0.08\) to
\(+0.07\) log-odds, so the efficacy gate fails at every size. That shows only that the
question mark does not hold the sum. The stronger test edits every position from the
question mark to the answer together: this block moves the answer by at most 6.4% of the
effect of donor operand digits (\(+17\) to \(+54\); 6.4% at 32B, \(+1.10\) [0.93, 1.27]
of \(+17.2\), and at most 3.4% at the smaller sizes). The downstream block is small
beside the operand edit, which is consistent with the answer re-reading the visible
operands; recomputation itself was not measured.

**Variable chains.** Sums are cheap to recompute. A chain of updates
(`a = 23`, `b = a + 4`, `c = b + 7`, ..., `What is e?`) makes recomputation at the answer costly and makes an indirect path the natural one. The running value could be passed from statement to statement, so this task was designed as a second positive-control candidate for an indirect path. It is not one. Donor states at the starting value's digits move
the answer strongly (at 14B: \(+30.9\), \(+18.5\) and \(+6.4\) for \(K=1,3,5\) updates).
Where single positions were edited (1.7B to 14B; at 32B only the block was run), donor
states at any later position, or at any statement end, move it by less than 0.4 in
absolute value. Donor states at *every* position after the starting value together, a
test that would detect a running value stored redundantly, move it by at most 4.9% of
the source-digit effect (32B, \(K=1\): \(+0.81\) [0.61, 1.03] of \(+16.5\)). The other
cell whose interval excludes zero is 14B at \(K=3\) (\(+0.44\) [0.08, 0.82] of \(+18.5\),
2.4%). At 32B the block is \(-0.02\) [\(-0.33\), 0.29] of \(+10.1\) at \(K=3\) and
\(-0.00\) [\(-0.22\), 0.19] of \(+5.2\) at \(K=5\). In the remaining size and length
combinations the interval includes zero. @fig-computed shows the \(K=3\) series, which
stays near zero. The downstream block is small beside the source edit, which is
consistent with the answer re-reading the chain.
Accuracy is consistent with recomputation at the answer. It falls steeply with chain
length, from 97 to 100% at \(K=1\) to 1 to 17% at \(K=5\) (Appendix
@fig-computed-extra). At \(K=5\), where maintaining a running value would make more
answers correct, the downstream block's interval includes zero at every size. That
agreement is correlational, not a test of what the model could do.

![Unwritten versus written computed values (Qwen3 variable chains), on one axis with two
denominators. *Unwritten:* the effect of donor states at every position after the
source, as a share of the effect of editing the source digits. *Written:* emission
divided by the total effect. 95% intervals. For unwritten chains (\(K=3\) updates) this downstream patch effect stays near zero,
which is consistent with the answer re-reading the source; recomputation itself is not
measured. *Written*: the share that goes
through the values the model writes (emission; \(K=3\) and \(K=5\)); the answer follows
the text. The remainder of the written case is the bypass to the edited
source. The two series cover different sizes because of which runs exist: both series
now cover 1.7B to 32B; at 32B the unwritten point comes from the block edit alone.](manuscript/figures/iclr_fig5_computed_and_written.png){#fig-computed width=100%}

**In these chains the answer follows the written values.** We return to the variable chains of
@sec-computed, now with the instruction "Compute each variable in order, one per
line, then state the value of \(e\)". The model writes each intermediate value.
The edit at the starting value's digits makes it write the donor's values in 86 to
100% of items. We cut the written chain after the second-to-last value and measure
the answer's first digit. The six-cell split then shows how much of the effect goes
through the written values (emission) and how much bypasses them (persistence with
the text fixed).

- Emission accounts for 92% and 96% of the effect at 1.7B (\(K=3\) and \(K=5\)), 93% and 96% at 4B (\(K=3\) and \(K=5\)), 94% and
  92% at 8B, 88% and 83% at 14B, and 98% and 101% at 32B (every chain usable after the parser fix).
- The bypass, which re-reads the edited source digits, is 4 to 8% at 4B and 8B and 12
  to 17% at 14B. At 32B it is \(+0.15\) [0.03, 0.28] (2%) at \(K=3\)
  and \(-0.08\) [\(-0.17\), 0.01] at \(K=5\). At 32B and \(K=5\), emission is 101% of the
  total because that bypass is negative. Emission plus the bypass equals the total
  (\(+6.62\) and \(-0.08\) sum to \(+6.54\)).

Written reasoning is not decorative in these models. The answer follows the written
values, and the part that re-reads the source stays below 17% at every size tested.
The couplets give the same picture on a smaller scale: the emitted line-2 words account
for 13 to 25% of the rhyme effect (@sec-couplets).

**Leverage.** How much of an effect goes through a written token depends on how much
that token matters. For a binary mediator \(B\in\{b_0,b_1\}\), such as the article *a*
or *an* before a planned noun, let \(q_i=P(B=b_1\mid I=i)\) be the probability of
writing \(b_1\) with the intervention off (\(i=0\)) or on (\(i=1\)). Let \(Y(0,b)\) be a
scalar outcome, here \(\log p(\text{planned noun})\), with the intervention off and
the mediator fixed to \(b\). Policy-weighted emission is defined as
\(E_{\rm emit}=\sum_b [q_1(b)-q_0(b)]\,Y(0,b)\) (Appendix @sec-app-sixcell). For a
binary mediator it equals, by definition,

$$
E_{\rm emit} \;=\; (q_1-q_0)\,\big(Y(0,b_1)-Y(0,b_0)\big).
$$

This is the change in the policy-weighted expected outcome, not the change in the
logarithm of the marginal probability. The effect through the text is the change in
what is written, times how much the written token matters to what follows. We call the
second factor the token's *leverage*. We apply the six-cell assay to the a/an planning
features of @hanna2026latent, which are selected by a rule with no article criterion.
We use their per-layer transcoders for Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B and reproduce their
node counts exactly on 297 to 344 of 349 prompts.

- At 4B, where they report planning, the features have a bidirectional,
  feature-specific effect on the planned noun. Of that effect, 92 to 94% travels
  through the generated article. The effect that bypasses the article (\(+0.012\)
  [0.000, 0.024] for amplified features) is at the level of randomly chosen features
  (\(-0.003\) [\(-0.019\), 0.013]).
- Stratified by leverage (Appendix @fig-computed-extra), the effect through the article
  scales with leverage, while the effect bypassing it stays small and constant. The
  article accounts for 53 to 82% of the effect in the lowest-leverage tertile and 94 to
  96% elsewhere.
- The product of policy movement and leverage predicts the effect through the article
  better than policy movement alone (correlation 0.886 against 0.831 for amplified
  features).
- At 0.6B and 1.7B the effects are small and travel almost entirely through the
  article.

Qwen3-4B. The effect on the planned noun through the article (vermillion) against the
effect bypassing it (grey), by tertile of the article's leverage over the planned noun,
for amplified and zeroed features.](manuscript/figures/iclr_figA_computed_extra.png){#fig-computed-extra width=100%}

# Settings built to favour relay: details {#sec-app-stress}

## Beyond the attention window {#sec-app-distance}

Gemma 3 alternates five local layers with a 1,024-token sliding window [@beltagy2020longformer] with one global layer [@gemma3]. Once line 1 lies more than 1,024
tokens before the rhyme position, five of six layers can no longer read it. We
insert \(D\) tokens of neutral filler, a seeded arrangement of fixed everyday
sentences, at the start of the model's turn, followed by a fixed cue (`Next line:`).
The model then writes line 2. The indirect path is split into three groups of
intermediate positions: the stored copy (the
prompt positions after line 1), the filler, and the generated text (the cue and
line 2). The committed decision number is the share of persistence that takes the
indirect path through the generated text: "go" at 25% or more, "stop" below 10%, and extension to 50
couplets in between. A full-attention control, Qwen3-14B, showed before the Gemma
result that indirect *shares* can rise with distance only because direct retrieval
weakens. We therefore added, before that result, the rule that a rise counts only if
the absolute indirect effect also grows.

@tbl-distance gives the extended run. At 2,000 tokens, Gemma 3 27B still writes a
rhyming line 2 in 82% of couplets, but persistence falls from \(+42.4\) to \(+26.4\).
The model reads less of the plan from the rhyme word: direct retrieval falls from 66%
to 40% of persistence. It relies instead on the stored copy at the line's final token,
which is necessary for \(+13.0\) [10.0, 16.1], about half of persistence. The absolute
indirect effect grows about thirteenfold (\(+1.0\) to \(+13.1\)), mostly through the stored copy.
The filler passes on nothing (\(+0.3\) by sufficiency, \(+0.15\) by necessity). The
indirect path through the generated text rises from about 1% to 12% by sufficiency (\(+3.2\) [2.2,
4.3]); its necessity is \(+2.7\), or 10%. This block contains the cue and all of line 2,
including its last three positions, so it mixes relay with the late lookup; the
split was not run. It is the largest generated-text block we measure, a borderline case
rather than a demonstrated exception: by the committed rule it falls between "stop" and
"go", and how much of it is relay remains unresolved. Even at 2,000 tokens it is a
minority path, about an eighth of the effect.

The window curve, committed before its result, predicted a change specifically
between 1,000 and 1,500 tokens. The interior distances use 18 couplets each and the
endpoints the 50 couplets of @tbl-distance, so the curve is not one uniform sample. It is only partly
supported. Direct retrieval is 66%, 64%, 54%, 40% and 40% of persistence at 0, 500,
1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 tokens, and the stored copy is necessary for 11%, 25%, 30%,
45% and 49%. The largest point-estimate step is where line 1 leaves the window, but the shift has
begun at 500 tokens, inside it. The indirect path through the generated text is 11%, 9%, 13% and
12% by sufficiency at the four nonzero distances (by necessity 10%, 14%, 11% and 10%): it appears once filler is present and does not
grow with distance. We therefore describe a long-distance shift toward the stored
copy, steepest across the window, rather than a precisely located window-edge transition.

::: {#tbl-distance}

```{=latex}
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
 & $D=0$ & $D=2{,}000$\\
\midrule
line 2 rhymes with line 1 & 98\% & 82\%\\
persistence & $+42.4$ [38.6, 46.0] & $+26.4$ [23.8, 28.9]\\
direct retrieval & $+28.0$ (66\%) & $+10.5$ (40\%)\\
stored copy: sufficiency / necessity & $+0.1$ / $+4.6$ (11\%) & $+9.7$ / \textbf{$+13.0$} (49\%)\\
filler: sufficiency / necessity & 0.0 / 0.0 & $+0.3$ / $+0.15$ [$-0.26$, 0.57]\\
```

Indirect paths at a distance, Gemma 3 27B (chat prompt; 50 couplets per distance; 95%
intervals). Shares are of persistence at the same distance. The generated-text block is the cue
plus all of line 2; it is not split into late lookup and relay.

:::

Three further models show what happens when lookup gets harder without a strong stored
copy. They also separate distance from the window.

- *Gemma 3 12B*, which keeps only a small stored copy (@tbl-storage), loses the plan.
  The window curve, committed before its result, predicted that the plan would
  survive while line 1 is inside the window (500 and 1,000 tokens) and vanish outside
  it. Instead, the plan fades gradually and is mostly gone inside the window.
  Second lines rhyme in 100%, 39%, 8%, 0% and 0% of couplets at 0, 500, 1,000, 1,500
  and 2,000 tokens, and persistence falls from \(+40.5\) to \(+11.5\) [8.1, 14.9] at 500
  tokens and \(+4.0\) at 1,000. At 12B the loss reflects the distance itself, not the
  window. No indirect path takes over: the absolute indirect effect stays at \(+0.8\) to
  \(+2.3\), and relay at or below \(+0.9\).
- *Qwen3.5-9B*, a hybrid whose attention layers have no window, also fades: rhyming
  falls from 92% to 4% at 2,000 tokens. What remains of persistence (\(+3.6\)) is still
  81% direct retrieval, and the absolute indirect effect does not grow (\(+1.2\) to \(+0.8\)).
- *Qwen3-14B*, with full attention, largely abandons the task after the filler (8%
  rhyming), and its absolute indirect effect stays flat (\(+2.3\) to \(+2.8\)).

Across the four models, distance moves reliance onto a stored copy where one exists,
and otherwise costs the plan. In no model does an indirect path through the generated text take over. The 12% in Gemma 3 27B is the unsplit generated-text block, including its last three positions. The rhyme word and the line's final token lie at
the same distance from the target, yet the global layers of Gemma 3 27B read the
line's final token. This fits the view of separator tokens [@chen2024sepllm] and label words [@wang2023labelwords] as summaries of their segment.

## Recurrent memory {#sec-app-recurrent}

Qwen3.5 [@qwen2026qwen35] interleaves three Gated DeltaNet layers
[@yang2025gateddeltanet] with each full-attention layer. A recurrent layer holds a
fixed-size state that is updated position by position. In those layers, information
from the source can reach a later position only through that state, passed along
every intervening position by construction and invisible in the text. The attention layers can still look it up.
The test therefore asks which path the model uses when both are available. We split
persistence by layer type. In the *attention-only* cell, the donor state enters at the
source, but the input of every recurrent layer at the source is restored to its clean
value, so the edit can move forward only through the attention layers. The
*recurrent-only* cell is the converse. A cell with both layer types blocked is a sanity
check. The rule committed in advance was "go" if recurrent-only is at least 25% of
persistence with its interval above zero, and "stop" if it is below 10%. It is decided
on the largest model; smaller sizes give the trend.

When the donor signal can enter at the source through either layer type, entry through the attention layers accounts for nearly all of its effect. At 4B and 9B (40 couplets each), the
recurrent-only cell is \(+0.28\) [0.07, 0.49] and \(+0.55\) [0.31, 0.79]: 3% and 4% of
persistence. The attention-only cell accounts for 97% and 96%. At the decisive size,
27B (48 recurrent and 16 attention layers; 24 couplets), recurrent-only is \(+0.41\)
[0.18, 0.64], 2% of persistence \(+18.8\) [16.3, 21.3], and attention-only 95%. As a sanity check, blocking both layer types at the source cancels the donor: that
cell is zero on every couplet, as it must be. Decision: stop. Although three
quarters of the layers can pass the plan forward only through the recurrent state, a donor signal
that enters through them at the source produces only 2 to 4% of persistence. The design controls
which layer type receives the donor signal at the source; it does not isolate every
later path through each layer type, so it measures the share of donor entry, not the
recurrent memory's natural share. Entry through the recurrent layers is small but
nonzero, which bounds the principle at 2 to 4% of persistence for this architecture.

# Hidden choice {#sec-app-hidden}

In every task so far, the content is visible: a reader of the text could recover the
rhyme sound from line 1, or the value from the operands. The case monitoring cares
about is content that cannot be recovered from the text. We create it with a secret
choice. The prompt reads: "Secretly choose one fruit from this list: {4 fruits}. Do not
write your choice yet. First write one sentence about the weather. Then write the
fruit you chose." Under greedy decoding the pick is a deterministic function of the
prompt. It depends on the model's own preferences and on the list order, so no reader
can compute it. For the path split, the model's turn is prefilled with a fixed
weather sentence and "The fruit I chose is". The outcome is the log-odds of the
donor's pick against the original pick at the next token.

**A small part of the pick-specific signal is stored after the list, and almost none passes through the sentence.** The donor is the same list in
another order, chosen so that the greedy pick differs. The reference is a *text swap*:
the donor order written into the prompt, which moves the pick by construction. In
Qwen3-8B, Gemma 3 12B and Gemma 3 27B (100 pairs each), donor states at the prompt
positions after the list move the reveal by 12%, 15% and 16% of the text swap. The
reveal reads all of it directly: the direct-retrieval cell equals the post-list effect. The
part of this stored signal that passes through the sentence is \(+0.00\) [\(-0.04\), 0.05], \(-0.06\)
[\(-0.14\), 0.01] and \(-0.01\) [\(-0.10\), 0.08]; it is also zero within its interval in
Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B. The rest of the pick, 84 to 88%, is not reproduced by the post-list patch; it is
presumably re-derived at the reveal from the visible list. The two largest Qwen models are the exception.

- In *Qwen3-32B*, the indirect path through the sentence is small but nonzero: \(+0.06\) [0.04,
  0.09]. That is 2% of the text swap but one eighth of the stored part.
- In the recurrent hybrid *Qwen3.5-27B*, the part of the stored signal that passes
  through the sentence is \(+0.03\) [0.02,
  0.04]: 1% of the text swap and one sixth of the stored part. Its sentence positions
  themselves account for 7% of the text swap (\(+0.15\) [0.12, 0.18]); Qwen3.5-9B gives the
same pattern (through the sentence 2%, sentence positions 8%). These are the largest in any model; Qwen3-4B has 5% and every other model at most 1%. This is
  expected when every position's recurrent state summarizes the prefix, including the
  list.

**What the stored signal could be.** An order swap cannot separate a stored pick from a stored copy of
the list order. In the out-of-list control, the donor list shares no item with the
original, so the donor's pick does not occur in the prompt at all. The committed
criterion is that post-list donor states raise the absent pick, and it holds in every
model. After the first results we identified a confound: the positions might hold a
copy of the donor's list rather than its pick. We therefore added, post hoc, *pick
specificity*: the effect on the donor's pick minus the mean effect on the donor's other
items. We then committed it, before the results, as the primary measure of a
replication in a second domain (animals; disjoint lists of six). The replication
confirms that pick-specific information is stored after the list, in both families
(@fig-stress C; @tbl-hidden). A same-pick null, committed before its result, gives the
converse check. The donor is the same list in another order with the *same* pick.
Post-list donor states then leave the relative preference for the pick unchanged on
average in Gemma 3 12B: \(-0.19\) [\(-0.53\), 0.16], against \(+1.01\) [0.78, 1.24] with
out-of-list donors. Gemma 3 27B gives the same null: \(-0.42\) [\(-0.96\), 0.10], against
\(+2.48\) with out-of-list donors.

These controls do not settle what the stored information is. The post-list positions
could hold the pick itself. They could also hold a copy of the list from which the
reveal re-derives the pick by applying the model's preference. Both accounts predict
pick specificity with out-of-list donors, and both predict the same-pick null. We
therefore claim only that information specific to the pick, and absent from the
visible text, is stored after the list and read at the reveal.

The families diverge with scale.

- In Gemma the stored share grows with generation and size. Gemma 3 stores 18 to 22%
  at 4B, 15 to 18% at 12B and 31 to 40% at 27B. The committed monotone prediction (4B
  below 12B below 27B) is only partly supported, because 4B stores more than 12B.
  Gemma 4 31B stores 82% (fruits; \(+2.93\) [2.56, 3.30]) and 91% (animals; \(+4.44\)
  [3.97, 4.93]) of the text swap's pick specificity. For Gemma 4 the path split was
  not run.
- In Qwen3 the stored share shrinks with scale: 10 to 15% at 8B, 0 to 7% at 14B and 32B.
  Qwen3.5-27B stores 3 to 4%. In larger Qwen models the pick is mostly not reproduced by
the post-list patch.

**The written sentence has no measurable effect on the reveal.** In the free version, the model writes its own weather
sentence. The sentence changes with the donor in 17 to 45% of pairs, but it never names
an item. Emission is \(+0.02\) [\(-0.03\), 0.08], \(-0.01\) [\(-0.07\), 0.04] and \(-0.00\)
in Qwen3-8B, Gemma 3 12B and Gemma 3 27B. The written sentence has no measurable causal
effect on the reveal.

**Where the stored signal sits.** Per-token necessity over the post-list block localizes the
stored information (@fig-sites B).

- In Gemma 3 27B, 77% of the pick-specific effect (\(+1.91\) [1.57, 2.24] of \(+2.48\))
  sits on a single token: *the* in "about the weather". With animals the same token
  accounts for 83% (\(+3.36\) [2.92, 3.80] of \(+4.07\)). The period after the list
  accounts for \(+0.42\), and the period ending the instruction \(+0.22\). Every other
  token, including the end-of-turn and role tokens, is \(0.00\pm0.05\).
- Gemma 3 12B uses the same site with fruits (*the*: \(+0.52\) of \(+1.03\); the period
  after the list: \(+0.32\)) and with animals (*the*: \(+1.04\) [0.80, 1.28] of
  \(+1.42\), 73%).
- Gemma 3 4B stores as much (18 to 22%) but places it mostly on the periods that close
  the list and the instruction (91% with fruits, 65% with animals), with a function word
  taking the rest (7% on *the* with fruits; 32% on *your* with animals).

The decisive check, committed before its result, changes the wording. If the storage
moves with the function words, it is storage at a predictable low-content token. If it
stays at a fixed position or spreads out, the site is template-specific. We reworded
the instruction to "Keep your choice private for now. Begin by describing today's
weather in a single sentence. After that, reveal which fruit you picked." Gemma 3 12B
then stores 12% of the text swap's pick specificity (\(+0.59\) [0.38, 0.81]), again on
two low-content tokens. The period that ends the list accounts for \(+0.42\) [0.21,
0.63] (71%), and the apostrophe of "today's", the token before "weather", for \(+0.16\)
[0.09, 0.22] (27%). Every other token is below 0.04. Gemma 3 4B moves the same way: the
apostrophe of "today's" takes 69% (\(+0.54\) [0.46, 0.62]) and the list-closing period
28%. Gemma 3 27B, where the base wording gave 77% on *the*, moves the same way. Its stored
pick specificity is \(+1.63\) [1.38, 1.88] (24% of the text swap's); of that, the
apostrophe of "today's" accounts for 82% (\(+1.34\) [1.14, 1.53]) and the list-closing
period for 23% (\(+0.37\)), which @fig-sites B shows as 75% and 21% of the row's positive
necessity. At all three sizes the site moved with the wording, from a function word to
the possessive token before "weather".

Across sizes and wordings, the stored information sits on two or three low-content
tokens. These are the punctuation that closes a segment (the list or the instruction)
and one function word or possessive token of the instruction, whose identity depends
on the wording (*the*, *your*, or the possessive before "weather"). Segment-closing punctuation is
the analogue of the line's final token for rhymes. In both tasks the model stores a
copy once, at a boundary next to the source or at a predictable token of the prompt,
and reads it at the point of use.

At Qwen3-4B, the forced sentence positions hold a small part of the pick,
\(+0.57\) [0.48, 0.67] or about 5% of the text swap. The donor run's sentence positions
read this directly from the list. In Qwen3 at 8B and larger and in Gemma 3 the sentence
positions hold about nothing (Qwen3-32B about 1%); in the Qwen3.5 hybrids they hold 8%
(9B) and 7% (27B, \(+0.15\) [0.12, 0.18]) of the text-swap effect.

# Relationship to an earlier workshop version {#sec-app-workshop}

A non-archival workshop version of this work introduced the emission and persistence
decomposition, there called public and private routes, on Gemma 3 270M and 1B with
sparse-feature and residual interventions on the article *a/an*. That version also
reported *mediator-relative routing*: target-directed interventions appeared to shift
toward emission when two alternatives required different articles. A
construction audit, frozen before its result, retracts that claim. The
named-donor direction contains an article-readout component, about 4% of its norm.
Removing it leaves lexical efficacy unchanged but removes nearly all of the
shift: the paired interaction falls from 0.120 [0.079, 0.161] to 0.018
[\(-0.000\), 0.038]. The component alone reproduces most of the shift. The shift
was therefore a property of how the intervention vector was built, not of the model.
The present paper keeps the decomposition, extends it to paths within persistence and
to multi-token generation, and replaces the small-model experiments with the study
reported here.

# Compute {#sec-app-compute}

Experiments ran on one Apple M1 laptop (16 GB) and one Apple M4 Max workstation
(128 GB unified memory), with no GPU cluster. Jobs were scheduled under a declared
memory budget and checkpointed per item, so interrupted runs resume without loss. A
27B to 32B couplet chain (screen, edit and generation, path split, position split and
necessity) takes one to three hours. The hidden-choice runs take 10 to 30 minutes
per model.
